This paper has received mixed reviews, with three votes for acceptance and one for rejection. While the AC acknowledges the concerns raised by the rejection vote—specifically, that the paper may miss a significant opportunity in the pathway to creating large-scale 3D implicit representations—the AC believes that the paper in its current form offers sufficient value for acceptance.

The AC concurs with the majority of reviewers that this dataset has the potential to be highly impactful, as it addresses a critical gap in the literature by providing a large-scale dataset focused on implicit representations. The AC is confident that this dataset could serve as a foundation for a broad range of future work.

comment.value:
**(Q) Compare with per-scene optimization methods.**


Thank you for suggesting the exploration of a more per-scene optimization pipeline. We present results for iCoMa, which is designed for Gaussian splatting, demonstrates greater robustness against larger pose errors. As for PI-NeRF, the code has not yet been released.

Following the iCoMa, we randomly added different levels of noise to the ground truth poses. The average result across 100 views is reported. 

|       Pertubation  $~~~$        |   Rotational Error   |   Translation Error  |  Converage Rate  |

|         max [30° ,  0.1]   |            $~~~~~~~$     0.007 °    $~~~~~~$         |          $~~~~~~~~$     0.005    $~~~~~~~~~$              |                $~~~~~~~~$  100%       $~~~~~~~$          | 

|         max [45° ,  0.2]    |           $~~~~~~~$     4.862 °    $~~~~~~$              |          $~~~~~~~~$     0.292    $~~~~~~~~~$            |          $~~~~~~~~$  88%       $~~~~~~~~~$              | 

|         max [60° ,  0.3]    |     $~~~~~~$     17.234 °    $~~~~~$        |           $~~~~~~~~$     0.876    $~~~~~~~~~$              |           $~~~~~~~~$  73%       $~~~~~~~~~$            |

|         max [90° ,  0.4]    |     $~~~~~~$     67.517 °    $~~~~~$        |           $~~~~~~~~$     3.125    $~~~~~~~~~$              |           $~~~~~~~~$  45%       $~~~~~~~~~$            |

Similar to iNeRF, the main limitation of per-scene optimization is its tendency to fail under poor pose initialization. A more robust approach for handling large pose errors is to first apply our feed-forward method to estimate the pose coarsely, followed by the per-scene optimization technique. The results of this approach are presented in Table 5 of the main paper.

**(Q)  Choice of INRs instead of GS.**


Regarding 3DGS, we had previously mentioned that we would **research 3D-GS as the next step**. As a matter of fact, we are glad to introduce our recent release https://arxiv.org/abs/2408.10906 in this direction.

In the current submission, we will add the 3DGS-related discussions. Please note that the interest of this work is not only 3D representations. Instead, generic neural implicit functions and their implied benefits (e.g. learnable tokens) are studied.

comment.value:
**(Q) Evaluation is limited to ViT-based methods; a broader range of models should be considered.**

(A) Thank you for the feedback. In Tab 2 and Tab 3, we present experiments using CNN models, demonstrating the performance gains achieved with our learnable tokenizer. Similar to deformable convolutions, our method allows the convolution to sample not only from a fixed pattern but also to learn sampling locations directly from the dataset illustrated in Fig 1. 

**(Q) Compare with per-scene optimization methods.**

(A) In Tab 3 we report per-scene optimization method using iNeRF (Yen-Chen Lin et al., IROS 2021) on out of distribution NeRF synthetic dataset, which can recover poses effectively only when the initial pose error is small. Additionally, in terms of time efficiency, per-scene optimization methods are computationally demanding (takes 16 seconds per pose), whereas our proposed method obtains the 3D pose through a single forward pass (requires only 0.06 seconds).

**(Q) Additional applications on 3D Generation.**

(A) Thank you for your meaningful suggestion. We conducted a simple experiment with generative models DDIM (Erkoç, Ziya, et al, ICCV 2023) to demonstrate the potential applications of our dataset. In Figure 1, we used DDIM to sample directly in the weight space of Omniobject-INRs using Apple class. After 2000 training steps, despite the high dimensionality of the weight space, our method was able to generate meaningful colors and shapes like Apple.

**(Q) Choice of INRs instead of GS.**

(A) We acknowledge that the 3D-GS method has several advantages over NeRF such like 3D-GS is very fast due to its rasterization and CUDA acceleration. We will research 3D-GS as the next step, but this paper focuses on INRs, so we chose NeRF instead of 3D-GS for 3D representation. This choice is made primarily to facilitate research in the weight-space learning and showcase the effectiveness of the learnable tokenizer in both 2D and 3D cases.  Please note that applying learnable tokenizer for 3D-GS is not trivial.

comment.value:
**(Q) More diverse scenes of data is needed.**

(A) Thank you for your valuable feedback. The current dataset we selected is object-centric, which limits the application scenarios of our method. We will continue to expand our dataset and consider incorporating more indoor and outdoor scenes, such as the ScanNet++ and KITTI datasets. More NeRF speed-up implementation will be used like instant-NGP.


**(Q) A symmetry-aware approach can be applied to handle symmetric objects.**

In Table 3 we report symmetry aware evaluation.
For symmetric objects, we achieve symmetry awareness by reducing the degrees of freedom in pose estimation, requiring the model to predict only the non-symmetric degrees of freedom. In other words, the pose parameters are recovered up the symmetry ambiguity in the given scene.
The results show that such symmetry aware approach effectively reduces pose estimation error.

comment.value:
**(Q) Concerns about computational costs and potential solutions?**

(A) Thank you for your feedback. Training 3D INRs requires substantial computational resources and time, which poses a significant challenge for us as we continue to scale up the dataset. Accelerated methods such as the Plenoxels(Yu, Alex, et al. CVPR 2022) approach and Instant-NGP(Müller, Thomas, et al. SIGGRAPH 2022)  may be used. In this paper, we used the vanilla NeRF to align with 2D INRs and to emphasize the effectiveness of our proposed learnable tokenizer.

**(Q) Multimodal can be used for improvement.**

(A) We appreciate your valuable suggestion. INRs can effectively represent various signals such as images, sound, and point clouds, which provides a solid foundation for extending our method to multi-modality. We will consider this for the next step in our research.

comment.value:
**(Q) The motivation for creating large 2D INRs.**

(A)  We agree that having a larger 3D NeRF dataset would be a significant contribution, especially considering the current trend of 3D GenAI. It is exactly what we are doing in this work and we will continue to expand our dataset. This being said, many benefits of implicit neural representation of 2D images are shown in the literature. Few such examples include, image inpainting (Sitzmann et al. NeurIPS'20), image compression (Strümpler et al. ECCV'22), image super-resolution  (Nguyen et al. WACV'2023). In this regard, our 2D dataset is expected facilitate further research in these direction. 
It is also important to note that the implicit representation allows to learn the token locations (both in 2D and 3D cases), as shown in the paper, thanks to its differential nature.  

**(Q) Insights of learnable tokenizer and pose regressor.**

(A) We are afraid that there is some confusion regarding the learnable tokenizer and pose regressor. 
We perform the tasks of image classification and segmentation in 2D, and pose regression in 3D. 
The choice of these three tasks are made based on the available labels and data volumes require for different tasks. For all three tasks, we indeed use the proposed learnable tokanizer. Please refer to Tab 2, 3, and 5 in main page (baseline vs. baseline+LP+Reg). We will clarify this.

**(Q) Other INR models.**

 (A) We agree that the standardization of INRs is an important aspect, especially with the emergence of various INR variants. Prior to the standardization, many research questions still remain. Two such examples include; weight-space learning and learning where to tokanize. Our dataset already allows to conduct research in these directions. Therefore, the need for standardization does not undermine the contribution of our work. We chose SIREN as the implicit function because it is a simple and effective approach, and it has already been adopted in many works [11-15] for weight space research. Additionally, many other INRs are built on SIREN, such as WIRE. As shown in Figure 1, SIREN performs well, while WIRE introduces some artifacts.

Furthermore, our proposed method leverages the differentiability of INRs, a fundamental characteristic of implicit neural functions. Therefore our approach is by design applicable to various types of INRs. We demonstrate this by generalizing our SIREN-trained model to WIRE, as shown in Table 1. 


**(Q) Expeirments on out-of-distribution test sets.**

(A) Thank you for your feedback. Following your suggestion, we conducted three sets of experiments for out-of-distribution tests;

1. Model trained on SIREN is tested on WIRE (Wavelet Implicit Neural Representations) for 2D

We generated CIFAR test sets in WIRE format and then used the trained model on SIREN (baseline + LP + Reg) as shown in Table 2 of the main paper. We freeze the model and the learnable coordinate, testing on WIRE model. The results indicate a performance drop due to domain shift, but the proposed learnable tokenizer remained effective.

2. Model trained on Omni-object and tested on NeRF-synthetic dataset for 3D

We generated 8 out-of-distribution scenes using the NeRF-synthetic dataset and tested our model (Ours + Pre + LP), which was trained on Omni-object-INRs as shown in Table 5 of the main text, on unseen classes and objects. While performance drops noticeably, our model still outperforms the per-scene optimization baseline method, iNeRF (Yen-Chen Lin et al., IROS 2021).

3. Model trained on CIFAR and tested on ImageNet (for overlapping classes)

We selected the classes from the ImageNet1k test set that overlap with CIFAR and resized them to 32x32, then we use the (baseline + LP + Reg) model trained on CIFAR and test on ImageNet, the results shows that our model demonstrates a certain degree of generalization to out-of-distribution data, with the learnable token proving to be effective.

rebuttal.value:
Dear All,

We sincerely appreciate the dedicated efforts each of you has invested in evaluating our work and providing invaluable suggestions, along with positive feedback on the motivation behind the dataset (**BRMW, yoA1, 7hMu**), its diverse applicability (**BRMW, yoA1**), and the effectiveness of the learnable token (**kysf, yoA1**). We have carefully addressed each question (Q) with detailed answers (A), ensuring that all concerns are comprehensively covered. All the Figures and Tables mentioned are included in the attached PDF file. Below are our shared responses to the reviewers:

**(Q) Limited 3D dataset in scale and scenes**

(A) We will continue to expand our dataset, particularly by adding more 3D scenes, including both indoor and outdoor environments, with the support of advanced speed-up techniques.

**(Q) Limited applications**

(A) We demonstrate a 3D generation example in the weight space, as shown in Fig. 1, and plan to explore this further in our future research.

**(Q) Insufficient baselines and other models**

(A) We have included out-of-distribution experiments in 2D using another implicit function, WIRE(Saragadam, Vishwanath, et al.CVPR 2023), and tested the CIFAR-trained model on ImageNet, as detailed in Table 1. Additionally, we report the 3D per-scene optimization method using iNeRF on the NeRF-synthetic dataset in Table 5. Furthermore, we implemented models beyond ViT, i.e. CNNs with learnable (convolution) coordinates, showing the benefits also in this case, as presented in Table 2.

title.value: Motivation for large scale 2D INR datasets need more justification

summary_and_contributions.value: This work proposes a large-scale dataset that comprises neural implicit representations for a few 2D and one 3D datasets. The authors showcase the benefits of this dataset via a few applications: (1) improved 2D classification and segmentation; (2) learnable token locations for transformer; (3) 3D camera pose regression with respect to NeRF model.

review.value:
This work uses SIREN to convert CIFAR10, ImageNet1K, and CitySkcapes to datasets of neural implicit forms and transform Omniobject3D to a dataset of NeRF representation. This work puts a lot more weight on the 2D applications of INRs by benchmarking classification and segmentation tasks. However, I'm not sure about the motivation and the value to convert existing image datasets to INR forms as INRs are not evidently better for downstream 2D tasks than just taking images. For 3D applications, NeRF and other 3D INR variances do have a superior advantange in terms of fidelity. Obviously, a large scale 3D INR dataset could be useful for a lot of generative 3D research. 

This paper demonstrates one of the benefit for large 2D INR data is to enable learnable tokenizer for transformer. The idea is interesting but  the experiments lack convincing evidence that the proposed RGB grouping schemes are better than other SOTA tokenization methods and generalize well to out-of-distribution test sets. 

For 3D pose regerssion on NeRF, the experiments also lacks more analysis. How does it compare against baselines like image based methods? Does it generalize to other INRs from different datasets?

strengths.value:
1. This work benchmarks using INR as a representations for 2D classification, segmentation tasks, and 3D pose regression directly on NeRF.
2. The learnable tokenizer is interesting and could inspire interesting research.

opportunities_for_improvement.value:
1. The paper seems put heavy weight on 2D INRs but the authors need to show stronger motivation on how converting popular large scale 2D datasets to neural implicit forms would be a preferred paradigm than standard images. It seems more valuable to have a large 3D neural implicit dataset for the current 3D GenAI research trend.
2. The focus of the paper is also not quite clear. This paper proposes learnable tokenizer for 2D INR and a pose regressor for 3D camera pose estimation by directly querying NeRF, which are both interesting but the authors didn't thoroughly investigate neither of the two directions to provide deeper insights. 
3. The paper should also discuss how to standardize and normalize INR formats as more and more new research are proposesd. Why specific INR implementation is chosen, e.g. SIREN or NeRF? If there's a new and better INR came out, would that render the old INR datasets useless?

summary_and_contributions.value:
(1) Implicit Zoo is a large scale dataset of neural implicit functions for 2D images and 3D scenes. It includes over 1.5M implicit representations, taking the time and cost of 1000 GPU days. 
(2) Not only Implicit Zoo covers 2D datasets but also include 3D datasets OmniObject3D. 
(3) The dataset can be used in multiple downstream tasks including image classification, semantic segmentation, and 3D pose regression tasks.

review.value:
Pros
(1) This paper provides a novel and large scale dataset for implicit neural representations.
(2) To ensure the data quality, strict quality control and refinement process have been conducted.
(3) The best way to validate the usefulness of a dataset is through downstream task's improvement. The paper conducted extensive experiments on various perception tasks.

Cons
(1) There were some regression in 3D pose for symmetric objects, not sure what was the root cause and if there is any way to address this problem.
(2) The way to obtain this large scale neural implicit dataset is very compute intensive, the paper did not discuss in details how to optimize for compute efficiency.

strengths.value:
(1) significance: The paper fills a critical gap in the field of neural rendering for implicit representation.
(2) relevance: A wide range of computer vision tasks can be benefited

opportunities_for_improvement.value: Multimodal: Considering other modality to make the dataset multimodal can be beneficial.

limitations.value: The authors have mentioned the concerns of high computational cost and potential negative societal impacts. However, they could provide more action items for addressing these issues.

correctness.value: The claims made in the submission seems to be correct. The evaluation methods and experiment designs are appropriate and well-executed.

clarity.value: Yes, the paper is well written and clearly structured.

The figures and tables in the article can fit the experimental conclusions. Therefore, the quality of this paper is sufficient to be accepted.

title.value: Well-written paper; but insufficient application and benchmarking

summary_and_contributions.value: Neural implicit functions are important in fields like computer vision and graphics, offering advantages such as high-fidelity representation of complex shapes and smooth interpolation. However, their development has been hindered by a lack of comprehensive datasets and the high computational costs required. To address these issues,  they introduce Implicit-Zoo.  This dataset includes diverse 2D and 3D scenes, such as CIFAR-10, ImageNet-1K, Cityscapes, and OmniObject3D. Ensuring high data quality, Implicit-Zoo facilitates research by enabling the learning of token locations for transformer models and direct regression of 3D camera poses from 2D images with NeRF models, thereby improving performance in image classification, semantic segmentation, and 3D pose regression. For evaluation, they evaluate various 2D, 3D models for classificaiton, semantic segmentation and pose regression tasks.

review.value:
This dataset allows 2D-3D unified task by connecting benefits from 2D and 3D superivison. In detail, thye 
For better data qaulity, they use additional skills (extended training) to ensure consistent convergence rates. 
There are many strengths of this paper but authors should enhance this paper. 
I have listed strenghts and weaknesses below.

strengths.value:
1. Clear writing: The authors have done an excellent job of clearly describing the concepts and steps involved in their dataset creation process, making it easy for readers to understand.

2. Descriptive captions and figures: The captions and figures in the paper are well-described, allowing readers to easily follow and grasp the core concepts and methodologies presented.

3. Clear documentation: The documentation provided is thorough and well-organized, ensuring that readers can easily navigate through the details and fully comprehend the work.

4. Strong motivation: The paper is driven by a well-defined and compelling motivation, providing a clear rationale for the research and its potential impact on the field.

5. Well organized experiments: though the number of experiments were insufficient, they have well organized the experiemetns to demonstrate the effectiveness of their dataset.

opportunities_for_improvement.value:
1. Limited evaluation: The evaluation of their model was limited to ViT-based methods. It would be beneficial to include a variety of models in the evaluation to better demonstrate the advantages of their model.

2. Comparison with other benchmarks: There are existing tools for evaluating poses, which sometimes require per-scene optimization. Reporting scores from these tools would help readers quickly understand the effectiveness of the proposed approach.

3. Limited tasks: Since their dataset can leverage both 2D images and 3D INRs, they could explore additional applications to demonstrate its effectiveness. For example, they could include generation models that take both 2D and 3D INRs as inputs and produce reliable 3D models. This isn't to say these experiments are necessary, but showing broader applications of their dataset would make their work more appealing.

4. Choice of INRs: It would be helpful to explain why they chose INRs over GS-based approaches, which also provide accurate and explicit representations that could enhance the model's understanding of 3D structures.

title.value: Implicit Zoo: A Large-Scale Dataset of Neural Implicit Functions for 2D Images and 3D Scenes

abstract.value: Neural implicit functions have demonstrated significant importance in various areas such as computer vision, graphics. Their advantages include the ability to represent complex shapes and scenes with high fidelity, smooth interpolation capabilities, and continuous representations. Despite these benefits, the development and analysis of implicit functions have been limited by the lack of comprehensive datasets and the substantial computational resources required for their implementation and evaluation. To address these challenges, we introduce "Implicit-Zoo": a large-scale dataset requiring thousands of GPU training days designed to facilitate research and development in this field. Our dataset includes diverse 2D and 3D scenes, such as CIFAR-10, ImageNet-1K, and Cityscapes for 2D image tasks, and the OmniObject3D dataset for 3D vision tasks. We ensure high quality through strict checks, refining or filtering out low-quality data. Using Implicit-Zoo, we showcase two immediate benefits as it enables to: (1) learn token locations for transformer models; (2) Directly regress 3D cameras poses of 2D images with respect to NeRF models. This in turn leads to an \emph{improved performance} in all three task of  image classification, semantic segmentation, and 3D pose regression -- thereby unlocking new avenues for research.

dateprocesses.script:
def process(client, invitation):

    domain = client.get_group(invitation.domain)
    venue_id = domain.id
    submission_venue_id = domain.content['submission_venue_id']['value']
    venue_name = domain.content['title']['value']

    now = openreview.tools.datetime_millis(datetime.datetime.utcnow())
    cdate = invitation.cdate

    if cdate > now:
        ## invitation is in the future, do not process
        print('invitation is not yet active', cdate)
        return

    def post_submission_edit(submission):

        updated_note = openreview.api.Note(
            id=submission.id
        )

        if invitation.edit['note']['readers'] == ['everyone'] and submission.odate is None:
            updated_note.odate = now
            updated_note.content = {
                '_bibtex': {
                    'value': openreview.tools.generate_bibtex(
                        note=submission,
                        venue_fullname=venue_name,
                        year=str(datetime.datetime.utcnow().year),
                        url_forum=submission.forum,
                        paper_status='under review',
                        anonymous='readers' in submission.content['authors'] or 'readers' in invitation.edit.get('note', {}).get('content', {}).get('authors', {})
                    )
                }
            }

        client.post_note_edit(
            invitation=invitation.id,
            note=updated_note,
            signatures=[venue_id]
        )
    
    ## Release the submissions to specified readers if venueid is still submission
    submissions = client.get_all_notes(content= { 'venueid': submission_venue_id })
    print(f'update {len(submissions)} submissions')
    openreview.tools.concurrent_requests(post_submission_edit, submissions, desc='post_submission_edit')
